title: Digging Into the Subsoil: Considering and Theorizing Human Services Delivery at the Sub‐Micro‐Level of the Public Service Ecosystem
authors: Kate Broadhurst; Steven Parker
affiliations: Loughborough Business School Loughborough University Loughborough UK; Department for Public Leadership and Social Enterprise Open University Milton Keynes UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Public services are often delivered in partnership with families and communities, yet these relationships receive limited attention within public service ecosystem (PSE) theory. Responding to call to develop the sub‐micro‐level of the PSE, we introduce the concept of subsoil sensitivity to foreground the family and community ecosystems that underpin public service value creation. These informal systems are active sites of value creation and destruction with sensitivities arising from their alignment or misalignment with public services. We propose legislative and policy nodes as connectors that translate macrolevel policy into microlevel practice. Drawing on child protection vignettes, we show how nodes create the conditions for interaction, while subsoil dynamics influence whether value is cocreated or codestroyed amid power asymmetries and differing belief systems. The paper extends the sub‐micro‐level of the PSE and offers a framework for examining family and community ecosystems in public service delivery.

title: Rethinking Supplier Integration in Humanitarian Supply Chains: Feasibility and Constraints From an International Humanitarian Organization Perspective
authors: Jihee Kim; Nezih Altay; Stephen Pettit; Anthony Beresford
affiliations: School of Management Anglia Ruskin University Cambridge UK; Department of Management and Entrepreneurship DePaul University Chicago Illinois USA; Logistics and Operations Management Cardiff University Cardiff UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the widely recognized importance of integrative practices in commercial supply chain operations, their application in humanitarian supply chains (HSCs) remains underexplored. HSCs differ from commercial supply chains in their relational dynamics and integration processes, operating under extreme uncertainty, demand volatility, infrastructural disruption, and resource scarcity across a complex web of actors. Using an embedded single‐case design, this study assesses supplier integration (SI) in humanitarian operations in a leading international humanitarian organization (IHO), as well as the IHO's relationships with eight key suppliers. Drawing on the relational lenses of power, trust, and commitment, distinct integration patterns were identified across different supplier types. The findings highlight humanitarian‐specific contextual constraints and are used to inform a typology of SI feasibility encompassing feasible, selectively feasible, and low‐feasibility integration. This typology provides a foundation for guiding supplier relationship management in complex humanitarian contexts. This study offers a framework for understanding how relational and structural conditions shape integration in humanitarian settings and underscores the need for IHOs to adopt context‐appropriate supplier management approaches that reflect the unique dynamics of humanitarian operations.

title: Looking the Part? How Candidates’ Race and Attire Shape Employers’ Hiring Decisions in a Low-Wage Labor Market
authors: Tiantian Yang; Jiayi Bao; Tianna Barnes; Ming D. Leung
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania; Texas A&M University; Dartmouth College; University of California, Irvine
abstract: Racial disparities in employment persist in the United States, particularly in low-wage labor markets in which employers frequently cite self-presentation, especially attire, as a basis for hiring decisions. Yet, whether improving professional attire yields equal returns across racial groups remains largely unexamined. Drawing on status characteristics theory, we argue that professional attire functions as an ambiguous proxy for unobservable traits such as motivation and reliability, making it susceptible to racialized interpretations. We predict that professional attire will yield weaker hiring returns for Black candidates than for their White counterparts and that perceived professionalism mediates this gap. We test these arguments using data from a gig-staffing platform comprising over 1 million job applications with profile photos, supplemented by a preregistered experiment that manipulates attire within candidates, using two photos of each candidate: one in professional attire, one in casual. The results converge across field and experimental data. Professional attire improves hiring prospects overall but yields substantially smaller returns for Black candidates. Moderated mediation tests confirm that perceived professionalism drives this disparity, such that race discounts how attire translates into perceived professionalism and how perceived professionalism translates into hiring. The racial gap attenuates in customer-facing roles in which appearance is task relevant. These findings challenge supply-side accounts of hiring inequality and reveal how a demand-side interpretation of equivalent signals perpetuates racial disadvantages.

title: Identification and Governance Strategy of Urban Systemic Risk Induced by Extreme Rain–Snow–Ice Weather in Southern China
authors: Wei Feng; Guirong Zhang
affiliations: School of Public Administration and Tourism Hunan University of Technology and Business Changsha Hunan P. R. China; School of Public Administration Central South University Changsha Hunan P. R. China; Center for Social Stability Risk Assessment Central South University Changsha Hunan P. R. China
abstract: ABSTRACT China's rapid urbanization has expanded urban spatial scale and increased the concentration of population, wealth, and infrastructure. Against the background of climate change, urban systemic risk induced by extreme rain–snow–ice weather (USR–RSI) in southern China has repeatedly disrupted critical infrastructure and public services, generating cascading impacts across interconnected urban systems. This study examines the generation and evolution of USR–RSI and develops a corresponding resilience governance strategy. Building on conceptual analysis, complex network theory and system vulnerability theory are integrated to construct the theoretical framework. A causal loop diagram is used to characterize risk diffusion and feedback mechanisms based on the 2008 and 2024 RSI disaster cases. Semi‐structured interviews and documentary materials are further analyzed using a structured data analysis approach to identify sensitivity and adaptive factors associated with node and path vulnerability. On the basis of these findings, a whole‐process resilience governance framework is proposed, covering resilience construction, integration of warning and response, rapid recovery, and long‐term adaptive optimization and transformative reconfiguration. The study provides an empirical and analytical basis for understanding and governing USR–RSI from the perspective of interconnected urban socio‐technical systems.

title: Hybrid Semi‐Quantitative Risk Assessment for Aging Offshore Platforms: A HAZOP–FMEA–Bow‐Tie Framework With Sensitivity Analysis and KRI‐Based Governance
authors: Muhammad Fawad Saleem; Majid Baseer; Qasim Tariq; Ahmad Khan
affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering University of Engineering and Technology, Peshawar 25120 Pakistan; Department of Engineering University of Palermo, Viale Delle Scienze, Building 9, 90133 Palermo Italy
abstract: ABSTRACT Aging offshore installations increasingly operate beyond their original design life, yet conventional periodic risk assessments capture barrier degradation only intermittently. This study presents a barrier‐conditioned semi‐quantitative risk‐assessment workflow that integrates Hazard and Operability Study (HAZOP), Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), and bow‐tie barrier analysis. The workflow combines decomposed residual likelihood and consequence scoring with threshold‐stability testing and a Key Risk Indicator (KRI)‐based update rule. Its principal contribution is the governance linkage: an explicit rule set that maps barrier condition and KRI threshold breaches to changes in residual likelihood, residual consequence, and risk band between formal safety‐case reviews. To ensure transparency and reproducibility, the workflow is demonstrated through a fully synthetic scenario representing a life‐extended semi‐submersible installation; all inputs are constructed and explicitly identified throughout as scenario assumptions. Under the illustrative scoring assumptions, a 19‐hazard register spanning seven hazard categories yields two high, nine medium, and eight low residual risks, with blowout/well‐control failure and hydrogen sulfide release remaining the highest residual risks. Per‐perturbation threshold‐stability analysis and distribution‐based Monte Carlo propagation indicate that 16 of the 19 residual risk ratings are sensitive to classification boundaries, suggesting that the reported scores should be interpreted as central estimates subject to uncertainty. The proposed workflow provides a transparent tool for risk screening and governance support, complementing full quantitative risk assessment (QRA) while preserving its essential analytical role.

title: Virtual Flood Experience Enhances Preparedness Through Emotional and Neural Engagement
authors: Toshio Fujimi; Takanori Kochiyama; Wataru Sato; Masahide Watanabe
affiliations: Disaster Prevention Research Institute Kyoto University Uji Kyoto Japan; Brain Activity Imaging Center ATR‐Promotions Seika‐cho, Soraku‐gun Kyoto Japan; Guardian Robot Project RIKEN Seika‐cho, Soraku‐gun Kyoto Japan; Faculty of Economics Ryukoku University Fushimi‑ku Kyoto Japan
abstract: ABSTRACT As climate change intensifies flood risks, strengthening individual preparedness is essential for sustainable societies. This study tested whether first‐person three‐dimensional computer graphics (3DCG) flood videos can complement official flood maps in motivating preparedness. We used these materials as operationalizations of experiential and descriptive information, respectively. In a preregistered web experiment with 1000 participants, those who viewed flood videos showed a small but statistically significant increase in preparedness intentions compared with those who viewed flood maps. Mediation analyses showed that, among the measured psychological variables, only fear had a significant indirect effect, suggesting that stimulus‐evoked fear helped explain this increase. We also conducted a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) study with 45 participants using a within‐subjects design. Flood videos elicited greater right amygdala activation than flood maps, consistent with fear‐related processing. Together, these findings provide convergent behavioral and neural evidence that first‐person 3DCG flood videos evoke stronger fear‐related responses than flood maps and that subjective fear helps account for their effect on preparedness intentions. The results suggest that visually vivid flood videos may complement map‐based communication by increasing emotional salience and promoting flood‐preparedness intentions.

title: Estimation of Excess Inhalation Non‐Cancer and Cancer Risk From Volatile Organic Compound Mixtures in New York City Nail Salons
authors: A. Michael Ierardi; Rachel L. Thompson; Samantha Fisher; Kimberly Anderson; Jean Grassman; Brian Pavilonis
affiliations: Department of Environmental, Occupational, and Geospatial Health Sciences City University of New York Graduate School of Public Health and Health Policy (CUNY SPH) New York New York USA; Center for Systems & Community Design CUNY SPH New York New York USA; Insight Exposure & Risk Sciences Group Boulder Colorado USA; Field Studies Branch, Respiratory Health Division National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health Morgantown West Virginia USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Nail salon workers are acutely and chronically exposed to mixtures of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), yet health risks in New York City (NYC) salons have not been systematically assessed. We performed an occupational risk assessment using integrated real‐time total VOC (TVOC) monitoring and chemical‐specific sampling of 11 VOCs across five NYC salons. Median and peak exposures and their 95th percentile (upper‐bound) values were used in non‐cancer and cancer risk models using deterministic and probabilistic approaches. Deterministic non‐cancer risk modeling indicated hazard indices (HIs) were generally below the benchmark value of 1, with exceedances observed only using upper‐bound exposures in the salon with the highest VOC concentrations. The probabilistic non‐cancer assessment showed a similar pattern, with some salons having non‐negligible probabilities of HI exceedance despite median HIs below 1. Deterministic and probabilistic benzene cancer risk assessments indicated exceedances of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) de minimis benchmark under multiple exposure scenarios. Although VOC concentrations were below occupational exposure limits (OELs), incorporating exposure variability and uncertainty identified elevated non‐cancer and cancer risks under certain scenarios. Previous research has linked nail salon work to adverse health effects, including respiratory symptoms and developmental and reproductive effects, suggesting that current OELs may not adequately protect this workforce. Our results highlight the need for improved exposure limits, chemical mixture risk assessment methods, and health protections for nail salon workers.

title: Urban densification to support climate adaptation: balancing costs and agglomeration benefits in the Netherlands
authors: Yashvant R Premchand; Peter Mulder
affiliations: Department of Spatial Economics, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam , De Boelelaan 1105 , Amsterdam 1081 HV,; TNO , Anna van Buerenplein 1 , The Hague 2595 DA,; Copernicus Institute for Sustainable Development, Utrecht University , Princetonlaan 8a , Utrecth 3584 CB,
abstract: Abstract Where should we build new housing under growing climate hazards? This study develops a framework that balances the economic benefits of density against the geographically varying costs of climate adaptation. We apply it to the Netherlands, where demand for new housing is high, but much of the land lies in floodplains or subsidence-prone areas. Agglomeration benefits are proxied by land values, while adaptation costs are derived from engineering estimates of flood protection and soil subsidence. Combining these data allows us to map spatial trade-offs and identify where development remains welfare-enhancing. Our findings show that dense cities continue to generate strong net welfare gains, even in places with high costs, while low-density settlements generate a welfare loss for new housing. We identify density thresholds above which housing development becomes feasible. Many medium-sized Dutch cities already exceed these thresholds, making densification more beneficial than peripheral expansion. Climate adaptation thus strengthens—rather than weakens—the case for urban densification.

title: Rethinking the Anatomy of Passion: A Biopsychosocial Configurational Perspective on Antecedents of Work and Entrepreneurial Passion
authors: Olivia Aronson; Marina Astakhova; Alexander Hamrick; Charles Murnieks; Henry Switz
affiliations: Robins School of Business University of Richmond Richmond Virginia USA; Bloch School of Management University of Missouri‐Kansas City Kansas City Missouri USA; University of Richmond Richmond Virginia USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite over two decades of passion research, our understanding of how passion is construed remains fragmented and dominated by additive approaches that treat antecedents as isolated predictors (both theoretically and empirically). Drawing on the biopsychosocial (BPS) framework, we challenge prior research by reconceptualizing passion as a configurational phenomenon emerging through interdependent BPS conditions which combine in complex ways to form equifinal pathways to passion. In doing so, we comparatively analyze configurations associated with harmonious and obsessive passion across the two most frequently studied domains in the management literature: work and entrepreneurship. To empirically examine this configurational perspective, we employ fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), which is well equipped to test the equifinal, compensatory, and interdependent nature of configural constructs. Using two time‐lagged samples of employees and entrepreneurs, we identify multiple distinct configurations that not only differentiate harmonious from obsessive passion but also distinguish passion across the work and entrepreneurial domains. Our results demonstrate that passion is largely domain‐contingent, such that work and entrepreneurial passion are each associated with mostly unique BPS configurations rather than universally operating antecedents. Our study advances passion research by shifting attention from isolated net effects toward a holistic view of passion as a system of interdependent BPS predictors.

title: Making agentic AI explainable and auditable
authors: Gongtao Zhang; Jimmy Huang; Jonathan Seddon; Miao Wang
affiliations: University of Nottingham; Audencia Business School Departement Entrepreneuriat Strategie et Innovation; University of Nottingham Ningbo China
abstract: Agentic AI promises operational speed, yet in finance, opaque decision paths hinder regulatory auditability. We address this autonomy paradox with a knowledge-enabled explainability (KEE) design theory that makes compliance an intrinsic, explicitly governed system property. KEE decouples probabilistic learning from an explicit, rule-governed reasoning layer, relocating epistemic uncertainty from opaque model inference to a semantic structure that can be inspected, contested, and updated. This enables ante-hoc structural control through a semantic, programmable graph that encodes regulatory mandates as executable, inspectable constraints. The theory specifies three design principles: structural knowledge codification, topological reasoning scaffolding, and adaptive synchronization. It also introduces six guidelines that operationalize regulator-acceptable, path-based audit trails. A longitudinal study of a multinational fintech platform provides naturalistic evidence that KEE can support high-velocity operations while producing path-based audit trails and accommodating controlled changes to regulatory logic. The study contributes to design science by theorizing auditable autonomy as ante-hoc structural control, specifying the entity-concept-event paradigm as its ontological mechanism, and formalizing this mechanism as a prescriptive design theory for regulated agentic AI.

title: How does a complementor develop capabilities in a platform-based outsourcing ecosystem
authors: Nan Zou; Chong Ma; Ilan Oshri; Ji-Ye Mao
affiliations: University of International Business and Economics; University of Auckland; ShanghaiTech University
abstract: There is ongoing interest in understanding how capabilities are developed by various actors in platform ecosystems. While much of the existing research has focused on the capabilities of platform owners, we know relatively little about how complementors build the capabilities necessary for their participation in ecosystems. In this paper, we argue that some platform ecosystems involve outsourcing contractual relationships between platform owners, complementors, and clients. This introduces a distinct setting—platform-based outsourcing ecosystems—which invites insights from the IS outsourcing literature. Traditionally, the IS outsourcing literature has assumed that vendors develop capabilities primarily through experiential learning in dyadic and mediated settings, with evidence for learning between vendors in outsourcing ecosystems. Building on this foundation, we conducted a case study of a complementor operating on the AliCloud platform to examine how capability development unfolds in such ecosystems. Our analysis reveals a learning process shaped by changing contractual relationships: the complementor begins with vicarious learning under subcontracting from the platform owner, transitions to experiential learning under direct contracting with clients, and finally adopts reciprocal experiential learning as a sub-platform owner working with other complementors. In each phase, the complementor assumes a distinct role that reflects its contractual relationships with other actors in the ecosystem. We theorise this learning sequence in a process model that explains how shifts in contractual positioning trigger corresponding shifts in learning mechanisms and capability formation. The paper offers implications for both the IS outsourcing and platform ecosystem literatures, highlighting how complementor roles and learning approaches evolve in response to contractual dynamics.

title: From a distance: How the social organisation of labour conditions personal attachment to work
authors: Anne Gravelle Antoni; Hamza Asshidi; Janna Rose; Nathalie Louisgrand
affiliations: Grenoble Ecole de Management, Grenoble, France; Université Grenoble Alpes, France
abstract: Employees are more often than not personally invested in their work. Such affective investment has been both praised as a potential source of self-fulfilment and condemned as a form of labour extraction. However, we aim to examine how employees in white-collar jobs navigate the multiple work and labour facets of their employment. Using the COVID-19 pandemic as a revelatory context, with the unexpected collapse of work-life articulations, we draw upon 50 semi-structured interviews of employees in a French private organisation of higher education. We show how individuals interrogated their investment in their employment as labour, yet not into their work as subjective endeavour. Moreover, we analyse how the material and social context of the social organisation of labour conditions individuals’ personal attachment to work. Finally, we discuss the struggle for a meaningful experience of working in higher education after decades of new public management.

title: Does the transition to self-employment benefit mental health? Evidence from the UK
authors: Liming Li; Karen Glaser; Ben Geiger
affiliations: Department of Global Health & Social Medicine, King’s College London, UK
abstract: There is limited research evidence on the mental health consequences of self-employment transitions from wage employment. This study fills this gap by investigating this issue using a difference-in-differences design with matching methods employing data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study (2009–2021). The results suggest that transitions to self-employment are associated with a small but significant decrease in psychological distress, signalling improvements in mental health. These effects are stronger among workers with poorer initial mental health when compared to their non-self-employed counterparts. Along with the self-employment transitions, workers also experience declines in socio-economic status but improvements in job autonomy, job satisfaction and satisfaction with leisure time. Overall, these findings highlight the potential protective effects of self-employment on workers’ mental health; however, caution is needed in considering the mental health premium of self-employment transitions.

title: Beyond Leaderism: Recentering Leadership Science Towards Relationships in Action
authors: Janaki Gooty; Chou‐Yu (Joey) Tsai; Tiffany Keller Hansbrough; Peter D. Harms; Sean N. Walsh
affiliations: UNC Charlotte; Binghamton University; University of Alabama
abstract: Abstract The historical origins of ‘Great Man’ theories of leadership, and their contemporary offshoots, have produced an accumulated literature in which the leader's behaviours are the focal unit of analysis. This Point article surfaces five theoretical assumptions underlying the leader behavioural paradigm: leaderism, individualistic attribution, behavioural universalism, democratization of leadership, and individual‐level ontology. We discuss theoretical counterfactuals to each assumption and call for a shift in the scene of scholarly conversation, from individual leaders to relationships that incorporate context and stakeholders. This shift in the focal unit of analysis from individual leader behaviour to relationships represents a foundational theoretical pivot built on multidisciplinary foundations, attention to levels of analysis, and a deep grounding in context. By questioning the assumptions underlying 85 years of leader behaviour research, we argue that the science (episteme), skill development (techné), and contextual judgement (phronesis) of leadership could be more tightly coupled by directing the spotlight towards relationships in context rather than individual leaders. In doing so, we move the focus from leaders in action to leadership as relationships in action .

title: The Ubiquity of Business Groups around the World: A Property‐Rights Theory
authors: Ruth V. Aguilera; Rafel Crespi‐Cladera; Alfredo Martín‐Oliver; Bartolomé Pascual‐Fuster
affiliations: Northeastern University; Universitat de les Illes Balears
abstract: Abstract Business groups (BGs) are collections of legally independent firms connected by ownership ties and are widely present in both developing and developed economies. We develop property‐rights theory (PRT) to explain this prevalence, extending its scope from the allocation of rights over a bundle of assets to the legal partitioning of assets as another allocative mechanism of property rights. Our conceptual framework complements traditional theories understanding BGs primarily as responses to institutional voids. Drawing on a large global dataset of firms, we examine how firm asset specificity and ownership sharing influence the controlling owners' decision to organize their economic activities as a BG or as a standalone firm. We find that the likelihood of adopting a BG organizational form over a standalone entity increases when (1) controlling owners rely on more firm‐specific assets, and (2) ownership is shared or potentially shared. Moreover, our findings are robust across three commonly observed firm strategic configurations: focused, vertically integrated, and diversified. Our study expands the PRT by developing a theory of property‐rights architecture, moving forward from the institutional voids perspective to explain BGs as efficient governance responses to asset and ownership complexities, hence contributing also to the strategic management and international business literatures.

title: Co‐Constructing the Illusion of Progression: How Boundary Blurring and Affirming Reproduce Social Exclusion in Elite Professions
authors: Stefanie Gustafsson; Laura Empson
affiliations: University of Bath; City University London; Copenhagen Business School
abstract: Abstract Social exclusion is a persistent problem in elite professions. While scholarship has emphasized structural and cultural barriers, less is known about the relational practices and mechanisms through which social exclusion is sustained. Drawing on interviews with 84 lawyers, paralegals, and managers in elite UK law firms, we develop a conceptual model of how the blurring and affirming of social and symbolic boundaries between higher‐status and lower‐status groups reproduces social exclusion. We show how both groups blur and affirm boundaries across three domains: professional work, professional space, and systems of professional advancement. Boundary blurring makes symbolic boundaries more permeable, positioning lower‐status actors as prospective professionals, while boundary affirming maintains social boundaries around professional membership. We identify and theorize the illusion of progression as a relational mechanism emerging from intertwined blurring and affirming, constructing lower‐status roles as pathways into the profession even though progression is rare. The illusion perpetuates liminality by sustaining hope, individualizing failure and undermining lower‐status groups' collective challenge to social exclusion. Our findings advance understanding of the relational mechanism through which social exclusion persists in elite professions, show how boundary blurring can sustain rather than threaten status distinctions, and help explain why organizational diversity and inclusion efforts have produced little substantive change.

title: Learning‐by‐twinning: Organizational digital twins and the future of search
authors: Prithwiraj (Raj) Choudhury; Yingxin Du; Megan Lawrence
affiliations: London School of Economics and Political Science London UK; Indiana University Bloomington Indiana USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs and managers often need to evaluate strategic choices, such as redesigning an incentive plan or entering an unfamiliar market, before committing scarce resources. Existing offline search tools, including mental models, analogical reasoning, model building, and simulation, allow managers to weigh alternatives without acting, but each is limited by what a single decision maker can specify, recall, or imagine. We argue that advances in generative AI, combined with the growing availability of firm‐specific digital trace data, are transforming this tradeoff. We introduce the organizational digital twin (ODT), an infrastructure combining firm‐specific data, AI‐based behavioral simulation models, and governance rules which facilitates a new form of offline search that we call learning‐by‐twinning: search conducted by observing how a strategic choice unfolds within a digital replica of the firm. We identify three mechanisms through which learning‐by‐twinning creates value, namely expanded search, safer experimentation, and richer system‐level feedback as well as specify certain conditions under which these benefits may attenuate. Managerial Summary Strategic entrepreneurship depends on discovering and refining opportunities through search and experimentation under uncertainty. Enabled by advances in generative artificial intelligence and organizational data infrastructures, we theorize that a new form of entrepreneurial search—learning‐by‐twinning—allows managers to conduct systematic virtual experimentation prior to real‐world implementation. We introduce the concept of the organizational digital twin (ODT) as the technological infrastructure that makes this search and experimentation possible: an evolving simulation environment built from firm‐specific digital trace data and multi‐agent AI models capable of reproducing organizational routines, interactions, and decision processes. We argue that learning‐by‐twinning alters the traditional tradeoffs of offline search by expanding the set of alternatives managers can explore, enabling low‐risk experimentation, and revealing second‐order organizational consequences before strategic commitments are made.

title: Backmatter of Theoretical Economics Vol. 21 Iss. 4
Frontmatter of Theoretical Economics Vol. 21 Iss. 4
Belief in mean reversion and the law of small numbers
authors: Jawwad Noor; Fernando Payró
affiliations: Department of Economics, Boston University; Department of Economics and Economic History, Universitat Autónoma de Barcelona; Barcelona School of Economics
abstract: Studies find that people systematically underestimate the likelihood of streaks in a random sequence. In a canonical coin‐tossing environment, this paper shows that the evidence can be explained by a belief in mean reversion. Such beliefs are represented as if the bias of the coin is history‐dependent and “self‐correcting.” In a Bayesian inference setting, a belief in mean reversion ensures that the agent never rules out the true parameter.

title: Information design in smooth games
authors: Alex Smolin; Takuro Yamashita
affiliations: Department of Economics, Toulouse School of Economics; Institute of Social and Economic Research, Osaka University
abstract: We study information design in games where players choose from a continuum of actions and have continuously differentiable payoffs. We show that an information structure is optimal when the equilibrium it induces can also be implemented in a principal–agent contracting problem. Building on this result, we characterize optimal information structures in symmetric linear‐quadratic games. With common values, targeted disclosure is robustly optimal across all priors. With interdependent and normally distributed values, linear disclosure is uniquely optimal. We illustrate our findings with applications in venture capital, Bayesian polarization, and price competition.

title: Combinator dynamics: Multidimensional evolutionary learning
authors: Srinivas Arigapudi; Omer Edhan; Yuval Heller; Ziv Hellman
affiliations: Department of Economic Sciences, IIT Kanpur; Department of Economics, University of Manchester; Department of Economics, Bar-Ilan University
abstract: In complex strategic settings with multiple dimensions, players often simplify decisions by breaking them down into separate dimensions. In contrast to standard replicator dynamics, which assume perfect multidimensional coordination, our combinator dynamics model captures cases in which players revise actions dimension by dimension, imitate successful traits in each dimension, and then combine the selected traits into a new action. We analyze key properties of these dynamics—monotonicity, stationarity, and stability. We then extend the model to heterogeneous settings, where some players imitate entire multidimensional actions while others combine traits imitated separately in each dimension. We apply the framework to organizational decision‐making, where decentralized adoption of practices can generate coordination failures, persistent performance differences, and a trade‐off between specialized and versatile organizational traits.

title: Contract terms monotonicity in matching markets
authors: Cyril Rouault
affiliations: CEPS, ENS Paris-Saclay, University of Paris-Saclay
abstract: We study doctor–hospital matching markets with contracts, in which hospitals can offer a range of contract terms to doctors. We show that introducing new terms can reduce doctors' welfare, whereas withdrawing terms may generate a Pareto improvement. We establish the preference domains under which welfare is preserved and show that only agent‐lexicographic preferences for all agents ensure that no doctor is worse off when additional terms are introduced. Since this condition is rarely satisfied in practice, our results imply that most real‐world markets are vulnerable to welfare losses when the set of contract terms expands.

title: Optimal auction design with contingent payments and costly verification
authors: Ian Ball; Teemu Pekkarinen
affiliations: Department of Economics, MIT; Department of Economics, University of Vaasa
abstract: We study the design of an auction for an income‐generating asset such as an intellectual property license. Each bidder has a signal about his future income from acquiring the asset. After the asset is allocated, the winner's income from the asset is realized privately. The principal can audit the winner, at a cost, and then charge a payment contingent on the winner's realized income. We solve for an auction that maximizes the principal's revenue, net of auditing costs. The winning bidder is charged linear royalties up to a cap, beyond which there is no auditing. A higher bidder pays more in cash upfront and faces a lower royalty cap.

title: Semistability in roommate problems
authors: P. Jean-Jacques Herings; Yu Zhou
affiliations: Department of Econometrics and Operations Research, Tilburg University; College of Business, Southern University of Science and Technology; Graduate School of Economics, Nagoya University
abstract: We study the roommate problem allowing for preferences with indifferences and agents remaining single. A stable outcome need not exist. We introduce semi‐stability, a novel notion that guarantees existence and restores stability through minimal policy or group interventions. We build an equilibrium foundation for semistability by showing its equivalence to a newly proposed choice‐based equilibrium concept. We show that undominated semistable outcomes are Pareto optimal and under strict preferences, every semistable outcome is Pareto optimal. Nevertheless, standard structural properties, such as the rural hospital theorem and the lattice properties, fail for semistable outcomes. We also discuss possible applications.

title: Selling information for bilateral trade
authors: Robert Evans; In-Uck Park
affiliations: Faculty of Economics, University of Cambridge; School of Economics, University of Bristol
abstract: We study the design and pricing of information by independent information providers for a buyer engaged in a trading relationship with a seller, and examine their welfare implications. While competitive information firms would sell full information about the value of the good, a monopolist supplies limited information in a particularly simple form—often resulting in higher total surplus than under full information, by influencing the seller's pricing decision. If only a single information structure can be offered, it takes a binary threshold form. If the provider can offer a menu of priced information structures before the seller sets a price, he offers a continuum of thresholds, inducing a unit‐elastic demand function for the seller. In both scenarios, the information firm increases total welfare when the seller's production cost is high but reduces it when the cost is low.

title: Collaboration between and within groups
authors: Matias Iaryczower; Santiago Oliveros; Parth Parihar
affiliations: Department of Politics, Princeton University; Department of Economics, University of Bristol; Center of Excellence for Negotiations and Analytics, BASF
abstract: We study the ability of multigroup teams to undertake binary projects in a decentralized environment. The equilibrium outcomes of our model display familiar features in collaborative settings, including inefficient gradualism, inaction, and contribution cycles, wherein groups alternate taking responsibility for moving the project forward. Expected delay grows more than proportionally with project size, and some welfare‐enhancing projects are not completed, even as agents become arbitrarily patient. A team composed of two equally large groups can complete larger projects than a fully homogeneous team, even as the difference in preferences for completion among the two groups is arbitrarily small. Moreover, if the project is sufficiently large, the two‐group team always completes the project strictly faster.

title: Informed communication equilibrium
authors: Frédéric Koessler; Vasiliki Skreta
affiliations: GREGHEC, HEC Paris – CNRS; UCL, UT Austin; CEPR
abstract: We consider a privately informed principal selecting a communication device to influence players' actions. In contrast to standard information design, the principal cannot commit ex ante, and the device must elicit information from all players. We define an informed communication equilibrium (informed CE) as a perfect Bayesian equilibrium outcome of this informed communication design game. We show that the set of informed CE is the subset of communication equilibria (CE) that yield principal payoff vectors bounded below by an equilibrium payoff vector of the silent game, under some consistent interim beliefs. The ex ante optimal CE may fail to be an informed CE. We provide sufficient conditions for a CE to be an informed CE and identify classes of games in which CE and informed CE coincide.

title: Repeated games with many players
authors: Takuo Sugaya; Alexander Wolitzky
affiliations: Graduate School of Business, Stanford University; Department of Economics, MIT
abstract: Motivated by the problem of sustaining cooperation in large groups with limited information, we analyze the relationship between group size, monitoring precision, and discounting in repeated games with independent, player‐level noise. The viability of cooperation under independent noise is linked to the per‐capita channel capacity of the stage‐game monitoring structure. We show that cooperation is impossible if the per‐capita channel capacity is much smaller than the discount rate. A folk theorem under a novel identification condition provides a near converse. If attention is restricted to co‐linear equilibria (a generalization of strongly symmetric equilibria), cooperation is possible only under much more severe parameter restrictions.

title: Strategic experimentation with privately observed payoffs
authors: Jérôme Renault; Eilon Solan; Nicolas Vieille
affiliations: Mathematics and Statistics Department, Toulouse School of Economics, Université Toulouse Capitole; School of Mathematical Sciences, Tel Aviv University; Department of Economics and Decision Sciences, HEC Paris
abstract: We study a strategic experimentation game with exponential bandits in which experiment outcomes are private. The equilibrium amount of experimentation is always weakly higher than with public outcomes. Moreover, in pure equilibria, experimentation is never significantly below the socially optimal level and may be strictly higher. We provide a tight bound on the extent of over‐experimentation. The analysis rests on a novel encouragement effect.

title: Nonparametric modelling of continuous-time Markov chains with scalable exact and approximate gradients
authors: Filippo Monti; Xiang Ji; Yucai Shao; Marc A Suchard
affiliations: Department of Biostatistics, University of California Los Angeles , Los Angeles, CA ,; Department of Statistics, Iowa State University , Ames, IA ,; Department of Human Genetics, University of California Los Angeles , Los Angeles, CA ,
abstract: Abstract Inferring the infinitesimal rates of continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs) is a central challenge in many scientific domains. This task is hindered by 3 factors: quadratic growth in the number of rates as the CTMC state space expands, strong dependencies among rates, and incomplete information for many transitions. We introduce a new Bayesian framework that flexibly models CTMC rates by incorporating covariates through Gaussian processes. This approach improves inference by integrating new information and deepens our understanding of CTMC stochastic behaviour by shedding light on potential external drivers. Unlike previous approaches limited to linear covariate effects, our method captures complex nonlinear relationships, enabling fuller use of covariate information and more accurate characterization of their influence. For efficient posterior inference, we employ Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. To avoid the prohibitive cost of repeated matrix-exponential derivatives under existing approaches, we develop 2 scalable strategies for exact and approximate gradient computation. Given N observations and K CTMC states, these strategies reduce the cost from O(NK3), with a substantial constant, to O(K3+NK2), with cheaper constants. We demonstrate the method in Bayesian phylogenetic and phylogeographic inference, showing strong performance on synthetic and real datasets and empirical quadratic scaling in K, even when N<K.

title: The Political Economy of Propaganda: Evidence from US Newspapers,
authors: Sebastian Ottinger; Max Posch
affiliations: CERGE-EI ,; University of Exeter ,
abstract: Abstract This study examines whether racial outrage in the media can result from the incentives of elites who seek to divide society for political gain, focusing on the late 19th century Southern United States. At this time, the Democratic Party had strong political incentives to incite racial outrage, and local Democratic elites exercised considerable influence over newspapers, the only mass media at the time. Using high-frequency historical newspaper data and difference-in-differences and triple-difference estimation strategies, we find evidence consistent with Democratic elites orchestrating a racist propaganda campaign to sway white voters. Supporting analyses are consistent with Democrats benefiting from anti-Black propaganda in the subsequent elections.

title: Agricultural Trade and Industrial Development
authors: Angus C. Chu; Yuichi Furukawa; Pietro F. Peretto; Rongxin Xu
affiliations: Department of Economics University of Macau Macau China; Faculty of Economics Chuo University Tokyo Japan; Department of Economics Duke University Durham North Carolina USA; School of Economics Huazhong University of Science and Technology Wuhan China
abstract: ABSTRACT Is agricultural productivity conducive to economic development? We develop a two‐country open‐economy Schumpeterian growth model with endogenous takeoff. With both agricultural trade and a subsistence requirement, higher domestic agricultural productivity has ambiguous effects on the economy's takeoff and its transitional growth rate if domestic and imported agricultural goods are substitutes. Without the subsistence requirement, higher domestic agricultural productivity delays industrialization and lowers transitional growth by increasing domestic demand for agricultural labor. This specialization force works in the opposite direction of the change in domestic consumption pattern governed by the subsistence requirement, which tends to release labor from agriculture. Without agricultural trade, the specialization force is absent and the subsistence requirement on agricultural consumption implies that higher domestic agricultural productivity reallocates labor from agriculture to industry, hastening industrialization and raising transitional growth. Using cross‐country panel data, we find that agricultural productivity has a positive effect on economic growth but this positive effect weakens and even becomes negative when reliance on agricultural imports is sufficiently high. Simulating the calibrated model, we find that improvement in domestic agricultural productivity accounts for about 30% and 15% of the changes in TFP growth in China and Japan, respectively, and more so for their main trading partner, the United States.

title: Marebito: citation matching interface for the digital library zbMATH open
authors: Madhurima Deb; Isabel Beckenbach; Norman Meuschke; Olaf Teschke; Moritz Schubotz
abstract: Abstract zbMATH Open is a leading curated bibliographic database covering approximately five million publications in mathematics. This paper presents Marebito, a production citation-matching system developed for zbMATH Open, and documents its architecture, domain-adapted feature design, and operational performance at scale. Marebito combines bibliographic parsing with GROBID, candidate retrieval with Elasticsearch, and a supervised Random Forest trained on domain-specific string-similarity features. Evaluation on internal zbMATH Open datasets yields precision and recall exceeding 98% on modern DOI-indexed records. Evaluation across two bibliographically distinct subsets reveals that classifier performance is strongly conditioned on metadata completeness, particularly title and author string quality, rather than DOI availability alone, documenting a concrete challenge for citation matching in mathematical literature. A preliminary comparison with Crossref on a manually verified subset of 2,037 entries illustrates the limitations of general-purpose matchers on specialist mathematical bibliography. A neural reranking baseline confirms that Elasticsearch-derived hard negatives are essential for abstention. We also discuss downstream bibliometric applications within zbMATH Open.

title: Is Informed Short Selling Concentrated in Family Firms? Evidence from a Reinvestigation
authors: FERHAT AKBAS; MINJIE HUANG; FELIX MESCHKE
abstract: ABSTRACT We reinvestigate Anderson, Reeb, and Zhao's findings that informed short selling is unique to family firms and driven by information leakage from internal disputes. Using the same firm sample and more comprehensive short‐selling data, we find that short selling predicts future returns in both family and nonfamily firms. We also find no significant difference in abnormal short selling before negative earnings announcements. In extended sample periods, short selling continues to predict returns for nonfamily firms under both ownership‐based and familial‐link definitions. Overall, our evidence suggests that short sellers are broadly informed and that family firms are not uniquely vulnerable.

title: Economic Fundamentals and Short-Run Exchange Rate Prediction: A Machine-Learning Perspective
authors: Ilias Filippou; David E. Rapach; Mark P. Taylor; Guofu Zhou
affiliations: Florida State University; Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta; Washington University in St. Louis and Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR); Washington University in St. Louis
abstract: Abstract The exchange rate predictability puzzle—that fundamentals fail to forecast short-horizon exchange rate movements out of sample—has long resisted resolution. We show that fundamentals do matter, but their effects vary with global financial conditions. Using a rich set of country characteristics interacted with global state variables and machine-learning techniques to handle the high-dimensional data, we document that interactions between country characteristics and foreign exchange market volatility are particularly important, consistent with a “flight to fundamentals” during periods of financial stress. Our forecasts deliver substantial economic value and offer new insight into the carry trade.

title: Housing Yields
authors: Stefano Colonnello; Roberto Marfè; Qizhou Xiong
affiliations: Ca’ Foscari University of Venice; University of Turin, and Collegio Carlo Alberto; University of Oxford
abstract: Abstract We build a granular data set of residential property yields using rental and sale listings from a major German real estate platform. With more than 1.5 million property-level rent-to-price ratios, we document a novel heterogeneity puzzle. About two-fifths of yield dispersion remains unexplained after controlling for extensive observable property characteristics and postal code-level time-varying factors using fixed effects. When we absorb finer neighborhood amenities through richer fixed effects, the unexplained share remains close to one-third. This evidence points to the importance of investors’ beliefs and preferences—rather than several alternative explanations we test—as sources of heterogeneity in risk premia.

title: Are the Hedges of Funds Green?
authors: Huan Kuang; Bing Liang; Mila Getmansky Sherman; Tianyi Qu
affiliations: Bryant University College of Business; University of Massachusetts Amherst Isenberg School of Management Finance; Baylor University Finance Department
abstract: Abstract Over the past decade, hedge funds have increasingly embraced green investing. We develop a novel return-based measure of fund greenness and find that greener funds earn higher average returns, consistent with capturing a positive green premium, and are associated with lower risks, especially during adverse periods. We further show that performance gains are greatest among directional funds, whereas risk reduction is most pronounced among nondirectional funds. We also provide evidence that managers of these funds exhibit superior green investment skills through green stock selection and green factor timing. Finally, investors reward greener hedge funds only when they demonstrate strong performance.

title: A Conditional Shrinkage Method for Portfolio Selection
authors: Nathan Lassance; Alberto Martín-Utrera
affiliations: LFIN/LIDAM, UCLouvain; Iowa State University
abstract: Abstract We develop a conditional shrinkage method for portfolio selection. Our approach builds on a decomposition of the mean-variance portfolio into the 1/N portfolio and an alpha component that offers large efficiency gains but is exposed to substantial estimation risk. We show that a linear shrinkage covariance matrix determines the portfolio’s relative exposure to these components, and our framework allows the shrinkage intensity to depend on a state variable that predicts their relative performance. We implement the method using investor sentiment and find that the estimated relation predominantly leads to greater shrinkage toward 1/N when sentiment is low, improving mean-variance efficiency while maintaining low turnover. title:
Demand‐Driven Propagation of Job Losses: Evidence from the Great Recession
                    <sup>a</sup>
authors: HA NGUYEN; JIAMING SOH
abstract: Abstract This paper presents evidence for the demand‐driven propagation of job losses in the context of the United States during the Great Recession. Using county‐level tradable job losses driven by aggregate shocks as an instrument, it shows that retail and restaurant (R&R) employment fell by 0.37% for every 1% of job loss in the rest of the county's economy. The finding is not driven by the house price decline or by credit supply problems. Moreover, the spillover is more severe for R&R industries that are most affected by consumer demand shocks during the Great Recession, which strengthens the argument for the demand‐driven propagation of job losses.

title: The Anti‐SLAPP Statutes and Corporate Environmental Policies
authors: KEVIN C.W. CHEN; ZHIHONG CHEN; CHENGZHU SUN
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; Hong Kong Polytechnic University
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether legal protection for civic participation affects corporate pollution. Polluters may deter public discipline through strategic lawsuits. Anti‐SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation) statutes mitigate this threat by enabling prompt dismissal and recovery of legal costs. Using a difference‐in‐differences design, we find that enacting an anti‐SLAPP statute in a state significantly reduces toxic emissions from that state by increasing local public pressure. The reduction is greater when the statutes provide stronger protection, when local stakeholders have stronger incentives and abilities to discipline polluters, and when local public pressure increases more after the enactment. Plants lower emissions by improving abatement rather than by reducing output or relocating emissions. Our paper underscores the role of legal protection in environmental governance and informs policy debates over anti‐SLAPP legislation.

title: Can citizen election observation increase public confidence in US elections?
authors: Jennie Barker; Oren Samet; Susan D. Hyde
affiliations: SNF Agora Academy Postdoctoral Fellow, SNF Agora Institute Johns Hopkins University Baltimore Maryland USA; Assistant Professor, Department of Political Science Rice University Houston Texas USA; Robson Professor, Department of Political Science University of California Berkeley California USA
abstract: Abstract Nonpartisan citizen election observation plays an important role in promoting the credibility of electoral processes around the world. This article assesses whether nonpartisan observation can shape attitudes among the US public, randomizing information about nonpartisan domestic observers in a series of survey experiments fielded to nearly 10,000 respondents. These included both hypothetical vignettes and information about a real‐world nonpartisan domestic observation mission undertaken by The Carter Center during the 2022 midterm elections in Fulton County, Georgia. The results show that information about positive assessments by nonpartisan observers of the hypothetical and Fulton County elections increased respondents' confidence in electoral results and processes, and also made respondents more likely to identify the officially announced winner over the candidate they favored as the candidate who won. Alternative ways of framing observers were largely inconsequential.
